strengths: Novel bridging of spectral representation learning with kernel-based CI testing through the partial covariance operator framework
Rigorous theoretical analysis with explicit Type I error and power guarantees (Theorems 4.1-4.2) with detailed proofs
Clear problem formulation and well-motivated approach addressing genuine limitations of existing methods (restrictive structural assumptions)
Theoretical framework implicitly adapts to diverse structural assumptions (smoothness, sparsity, low-rank) without explicit modeling
Well-written paper with good intuition and clear presentation of technical content
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only one synthetic benchmark (post-nonlinear model), no real data experiments despite claims of practicality and scalability
Critical gap between theory and practice: core assumption E_m → 0 (Eq. 9) is assumed but never proven for Algorithm 1; no convergence rate established for representation learning error
Scalability claims (Abstract, Intro, Conclusion) are entirely unsubstantiated—no computational complexity analysis, no timing comparisons, no GPU acceleration evidence provided

Stringent and partially unvalidated theoretical assumptions: Assumption 4.1 (sub-Gaussianity of learned features) never verified; sample complexity requirement n ≥ cK⁴d² log n is very restrictive with unknown constant c

Significant theory-practice gap: no practical guidance for choosing dimension d, verifying power conditions, or setting hyperparameters; Algorithm 1 has many unspecified design choices with no ablation studies

Representation learning convergence not empirically studied: no demonstration that Algorithm 1 achieves small E_m, no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters, no validation that sub-Gaussianity holds for learned features
Limited baseline comparisons and missing analyses: no real-world applications, no computational time comparisons, no robustness studies across different distributional assumptions
Algorithm design appears partially ad-hoc: whitening post-processing after orthonormality regularization motivation unclear; symmetrization of N_θ not justified

strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework with asymptotic validity (Theorem 4.1) and power guarantees (Theorem 4.2) for the test statistic
Principled derivation of bi-level optimization formulation from Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem, elegantly connecting kernel methods with spectral representation learning
Well-motivated problem addressing fundamental challenges in CI testing (Shah & Peters no-free-lunch result) with clear practical examples
Comprehensive technical analysis with detailed proofs; non-trivial extension of Kostic et al. (2024) to partial covariance operators
Concrete, implementable algorithm with thoughtful design choices (orthonormality regularization, whitening post-processing)
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only synthetic data on single model, no real data, no timing/scalability analysis, no evidence of practical advantage over KCIT/RCIT/GCIT despite scalability claims

Critical gap between theory and practice: Theory assumes E_m → 0 but provides no convergence rates, finite-sample bounds, or analysis of Algorithm 1 convergence; whitening post-processing not covered by theoretical guarantees
Strong unjustified assumptions: Assumption 4.1 (sub-Gaussianity of learned features) is assumed but never empirically verified; Assumption 3.1 sufficient conditions are non-trivial

Missing practical guidance: No principled method for selecting d, no hyperparameter selection guidance, no analysis of sample complexity m needed to achieve target E_m, no computational complexity analysis

Algorithm complexity concerns: Bi-level optimization with competing objectives (orthonormality regularization vs. main loss), suggesting suboptimal solutions requiring post-hoc whitening; unknown sensitivity to network architecture and hyperparameter choices

Asymptotic theory with restrictive conditions: Theorems are asymptotic only; regime d = o(√n) is limiting; power bound ε²_n ≥ 2dE²_m + cd²+log(δ⁻¹)/n can be stringent for weak signals, especially with non-negligible E_m
Limited novelty: Core spectral representation learning approach closely follows Kostic et al. (2024); main contribution is bi-level extension to partial covariance, which is somewhat incremental

strengths: Novel methodological approach bridging kernel-based theory with spectral representation learning for CI testing, addressing real scalability and assumptions limitations of existing methods
Rigorous theoretical framework with explicit connections between representation learning error and test performance; Theorems 4.1-4.2 establish asymptotic validity and power guarantees
Comprehensive and honest analysis with extensive proofs, ablation studies, and detailed treatment of limitations; acknowledgment of open problems (explicit rates for E_m)

Strong experimental validation across multiple synthetic benchmarks and real data; demonstrates robustness to non-smooth distributions violating competitors' assumptions; ~2× computational speedup over KCIT
Practical utility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Figs. 6-8), and thorough reproducibility documentation enabling adoption
Maintains Type I error control in high-dimensional settings where kernel-based methods fail, with competitive or superior power in most scenarios
weaknesses: Fundamental theory-practice gap: asymptotic guarantees critically depend on uncharacterized representation learning error (E_m). No explicit rates provided for E_m as a function of architecture, sample size, or optimization quality; paper acknowledges this as 'open problem beyond our specific method', severely limiting practical applicability of theory

Conservative calibration observed in practice, especially on high-dimensional benchmark (Fig. 10: Type I error ~0.1 at α=0.05); gap between theory (χ² asymptotic distribution) and empirical behavior unexplained, reducing power and practical utility

Limited novelty in individual components: Algorithm 1 is primarily an extension of Kostic et al. (2024) via bi-level formulation; test statistic (Eq. 10) is standard; representation learning framework unoriginal. Main novelty lies in application rather than methodology

Experimental concerns: (1) Hyperparameter tuning may not be fair—baselines tuned with fixed budgets rather than optimally; DGCIT particularly disadvantaged as architectural hyperparameters not exposed. (2) LPCIT excluded due to 'excessive runtime' without actual timing data. (3) Breast cancer application limited to 135 WSIs, insufficient for strong conclusions. (4) Conservative behavior on high-dimensional benchmark suggests possible overfitting to original benchmarks

Theory-practice gap on key conditions: Assumption 4.1 requires bounded activations (Tanh) but no sensitivity analysis; condition d = o(√n) restrictive for very high-dimensional settings; Lemma B.3's conditions (√d E^θ_m → 0) stated but not justified; sufficient condition in Theorem 4.2 non-constructive with unspecified constants

Missing key comparisons: diffusion-based CI test (Yang et al., 2025) mentioned but not experimentally compared; LPCIT excluded without runtime comparison; recent kernel selection work (Wang et al., 2026) only cited in passing

strengths: Novel bi-level contrastive learning formulation elegantly handles the unobservable composition ΣXZΣZY̅ via a rank-2d auxiliary problem—a clever technical solution

Rigorous theoretical analysis: Theorem 4.1 establishes asymptotic normality (χ²(d²) limiting distribution) under null; Theorem 4.2 characterizes power with explicit dependence on representation error; proofs are technically sound

Addresses real limitations of kernel-based CI tests (KCIT, RCIT) by achieving better scalability while maintaining validity—demonstrated to work in high-dimensional settings (d_Z=300) where competitors fail

Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple benchmarks (post-nonlinear, nonsmooth high-dimensional, real breast cancer data), thorough baseline comparisons, type I error control, ~2× computational speedup, and sensitivity analyses on key hyperparameters
Well-motivated combination of classical operator-based framework with modern neural representation learning, bridging two important areas in a principled way
Clear, well-organized presentation with effective visualizations of methodology and empirical findings; comprehensive appendix with full proofs
weaknesses: Theoretical validity and power guarantees depend critically on E^val_m → 0 and scaling of E^pow_m, but no non-asymptotic convergence rates are provided for these quantities—acknowledged as 'open problem' but creates gap between asymptotic theory and finite-sample practice
Regime restrictions (d = o(√n), √d E_m → 0, n ≥ cK⁴d² log n) are demanding without explicit rates for E_m; unclear how neural architecture and training dynamics affect convergence in practice

Empirical limitations: (1) most experiments use small sample sizes (N=1000); (2) conservative calibration in practice reduces power by unquantified amount; (3) hyperparameter tuning via 30 Bayesian trials remains somewhat arbitrary despite efforts to standardize across methods

Post-hoc dimension pruning (Section C) introduces additional hyperparameter and feels ad-hoc; whitening post-processing necessary despite orthonormality regularization, suggesting potential optimization fragility
Bi-level optimization not theoretically analyzed: no convergence guarantees, single inner/outer updates per iteration may not achieve good minima, approximation errors not characterized

Limited scope: (1) continuous variables only, no discrete/mixed settings; (2) only small-scale causal discovery experiments (Table 6) despite claims about bridging to constraint-based discovery; (3) constants in power theorem hidden, making practical detectability unclear
